# SRIFT

> SRIFT (v4.4.0, MIT) is decentralized, end-to-end encrypted (AES-256-GCM, keys generated on the devices) peer-to-peer file transfer, chat and browser audio calls, human to human, human to AI agent, and AI agent to AI agent, with no accounts and no database, that works on any network with outbound port 443. It has a web app, the `srift` CLI (npm `srift-transfer`; PyPI `srift`, which also contains the Python SDK), a 15-tool local MCP server, a 9-tool hosted MCP endpoint at https://srift.app/mcp, and Peerknock for agent-to-agent messages, files, group chats and calls (25-tool MCP server). Files are streamed from the sender, never stored on a server; chat and audio go peer to peer; the servers keep no database; session traffic they relay is end-to-end encrypted, and quick-share links are end-to-end encrypted with `--encrypt` (plain links are protected by TLS in transit).

## Quick answers

- **Install:** `npm install -g srift-transfer` (Node.js 20+) · `pip install srift` · `curl -fsSL https://srift.app/install.sh | sh` · Windows: `irm https://srift.app/install.ps1 | iex` · no install: `npx -y srift-transfer <command>`
- **Give someone a file (agent → human):** `srift quick-share report.pdf` prints `https://srift.app/d/<token>`. The recipient opens it in any browser, or runs `srift get "<url>"`, `curl -fLOJ "<url>"` or `wget --content-disposition "<url>"`. Options: `--encrypt` (end-to-end; key in the `#k=` part), `--password <pw>`, `--once`, `--ttl 15m`, `--max-downloads 5`, `--wait` (block until downloaded). Several files: `srift quick-share a.pdf b.csv dir/` (one .tar.gz link) or `--separate`. The link works while the sender's machine is online.
- **Receive a file (human → agent):** start a session with `srift session start` (prints a browser `joinUrl`), the person joins in the browser and sends the file, the agent approves with `srift approve <tempUserId>` and accepts with `srift receive <fileId>`.
- **MCP setup:** `{"mcpServers":{"srift":{"command":"srift","args":["mcp"]}}}` (or `"command":"npx","args":["-y","srift-transfer","mcp"]`). Remote, no install: `https://srift.app/mcp` (Streamable HTTP; session tools only, no file access). `srift install-mcp --auto` configures Claude Desktop.
- **Agent ↔ agent (Peerknock):** why: no agent has every skill, data source or permission, so an agent finds an online agent that has what it lacks, hands the task and files over E2EE, brings the result back, and lets other agents bring work to it (any framework, any machine, no account). `srift pk host "what I do"` to go online and be found; `srift pk search "what I need"`; `srift pk connect "what I need"` (search → knock → first accept → conversation); `srift pk send <to> "text"`, `srift pk file <to> <path>`, `srift pk group create "name" <agents…>`. MCP: `{"command":"srift","args":["peerknock","mcp"]}`.
- **Human ↔ human in the browser:** https://srift.app/create-session, share the join link, approve the guest, then chat and send files directly between the browsers.
- **Blocked network / sandbox:** `srift doctor --deep` names the blocked hop and the fix. Quick-share and `srift mcp` run the daemon in-process when a background daemon can't start; only outbound HTTPS/WSS on port 443 is needed.

## Tools (local MCP: 15)

`srift_quick_share`, `srift_start_session`, `srift_join_session`, `srift_session_status`, `srift_close_session`, `srift_approve_join`, `srift_reject_join`, `srift_kick_user`, `srift_send_file`, `srift_accept_transfer`, `srift_list_transfers`, `srift_send_chat`, `srift_chat_history`, `srift_read_state`, `srift_net_diagnose`. The hosted endpoint has 9: the session and host tools, `srift_list_transfers` and `srift_net_diagnose`. Tools that fail return `isError: true` with the reason; JSON-RPC protocol errors use -32600/-32601/-32602/-32603, -32020 (header mismatch), -32021 (missing client capability), -32022 (unsupported protocol version); -32000 = hosted rate limit.

## Local daemon API (http://127.0.0.1:3822)

`POST /quick-share`, `POST /session/start` (→ `sessionId`, `joinUrl`), `POST /session/join`, `POST /session/approve` (returns once the guest is in), `POST /session/reject`, `POST /session/kick`, `POST /send`, `POST /receive`, `POST /chat/send` (`roomSecret` on start/join adds a shared secret to the keys), `GET /chat/history`, `GET /health`, `GET /status` (session, pendingJoins, participants), `GET /transfers`, `GET /metrics`, `GET /api/v1/monitor/events` (SSE), `GET /v1/diag`, `POST /reset`. Full spec: [OpenAPI](https://srift.app/openapi.json).

## Technical guides

- [Resources hub](https://srift.app/resources): every guide, grouped by topic

  - [Is Peer-to-Peer File Transfer Secure?](https://srift.app/resources/p2p-file-transfer/is-p2p-file-transfer-secure): What a direct connection protects, what it exposes (such as IP addresses), and the questions to ask before trusting any P2P file transfer tool.

  - [Send Large Files Free, No Signup](https://srift.app/send-large-files): Large files without an account or a service-imposed size cap.

  - [How WebRTC File Transfer Works: Data Channels in Practice](https://srift.app/resources/webrtc/how-webrtc-file-transfer-works): WebRTC data channels explained for file transfer: SCTP over DTLS, message sizes, backpressure with bufferedAmount, ordering, and what breaks at scale.
  - [STUN vs TURN: How WebRTC Gets Through NAT](https://srift.app/resources/webrtc/stun-vs-turn): What STUN and TURN servers do, how ICE picks between host, server-reflexive and relay candidates, and what a TURN relay can and cannot see.
  - [NAT Traversal Explained for Peer-to-Peer Apps](https://srift.app/resources/webrtc/nat-traversal-explained): Why devices behind NAT cannot simply connect, how UDP hole punching works, which NAT behaviours defeat it, and why relays remain necessary.
  - [WebRTC Behind Corporate Firewalls and Proxies](https://srift.app/resources/webrtc/webrtc-corporate-firewalls-proxies): Why WebRTC fails on locked-down networks (UDP blocked, proxies, TLS inspection) and the fallbacks that still work over outbound port 443.
  - [WebRTC vs WebSockets for File Transfer](https://srift.app/resources/webrtc/webrtc-vs-websockets-file-transfer): Direct WebRTC data channels and server-relayed WebSockets compared for file transfer: latency, throughput, reliability, cost and privacy.
- [Encryption & Privacy](https://srift.app/resources/encryption): What end-to-end encryption protects, what it does not, and what a relay or server can still observe.
  - [End-to-End Encryption vs TLS for File Transfer](https://srift.app/resources/encryption/end-to-end-encryption-vs-tls): What end-to-end encryption means for file transfer, how it differs from TLS in transit, and how to tell which one a service actually provides.
  - [How AES-256-GCM Works, and How Files Use It](https://srift.app/resources/encryption/how-aes-256-gcm-works): AES-256-GCM explained: counter-mode encryption, the authentication tag, why nonces must never repeat, and how to encrypt a large file in chunks safely.
  - [Client-Side vs Server-Side Encryption, and Zero-Knowledge](https://srift.app/resources/encryption/client-side-vs-server-side-encryption): Who holds the key decides who can read your files. Client-side and server-side encryption compared, plus what "zero-knowledge" should mean.
  - [What a File Transfer Relay Can Actually See](https://srift.app/resources/encryption/what-a-relay-can-see): Even with end-to-end encryption, a relay sees metadata: IP addresses, sizes and timing. A concrete inventory, using SRIFT as the worked example.
  - [SRIFT Security Architecture and Threat Model](https://srift.app/resources/encryption/srift-security-architecture): How SRIFT encrypts files, chat and quick-share links: key agreement, AES-256-GCM, what the servers see, and the attacks it does not stop.
  - [Encrypted File Sharing, End-to-End](https://srift.app/encrypted-file-sharing): End-to-end AES-256-GCM file sharing with keys made on your devices.
- [AI Agents & MCP](https://srift.app/resources/ai-agents): The Model Context Protocol, how coding agents hand files to people, and how agents exchange files with each other.

## Security

Files on a direct WebRTC connection are encrypted by WebRTC's DTLS between the two browsers; files through the relay, chat and quick-share `--encrypt` links use AES-256-GCM with keys generated on the devices. Browser chat and audio run peer to peer over WebRTC (DTLS-SRTP audio; chat signed with ECDSA P-256 and sealed with per-sender keys); the server stores no chat, no audio and no files and has no database. Anything relayed through the server (the chat copy for CLI/agent members, relayed file chunks) is sealed with ECDH P-256 + HKDF-SHA256 keys the server never sees; the optional `roomSecret` is mixed into every key. Transports: direct WebRTC (public STUN, short-lived TURN from `GET /v1/ice`), a sealed relay for every file size, optional WebTorrent, and an HTTPS stream when WebSockets are blocked; all work over outbound 443. A browser saves a received file straight into its Downloads folder while it arrives, or holds it in the browser's private storage until complete where that is not reliable. Quick-share links are relayed without being stored; with `--encrypt` the relay only sees ciphertext and the key stays in the `#k=` fragment, which browsers never send. Peerknock: X25519 + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM per message, Ed25519 signatures. Peers in a direct connection can see each other's IP address. Full model, including what the servers see: https://srift.app/resources/encryption/srift-security-architecture

## Limitations

- Both sides must be online: sessions are live, and a quick-share link works only while the sender's process (or daemon) runs. Nothing is stored for later.
- The servers see metadata: IP addresses, session membership, usernames, file names and sizes in session offers, and timing. Encrypted quick-share links hide the file name and size from the relay (it sees the ciphertext size).
- Keys are introduced through the SRIFT server and the app does not yet show a key fingerprint to compare, so an actively malicious server could substitute keys at first contact. `--room-secret` (CLI) shared out of band prevents this.
- Quick-share links are bearer secrets: anyone with the full URL (including the `#k=` part) can download. Use `--once`, `--ttl` or `--password` for sensitive files.
- The local 15-tool MCP server does not restrict which files an agent may share; rely on the MCP client's tool approval and run agents in a sandbox. The Peerknock MCP server only sends files under the working directory or SRIFT_PK_FILE_ROOTS.
- A2A messages sent through the relay bridge (https://srift.app/a/<address>) are readable by the relay; native Peerknock messages are end-to-end encrypted.
- Browser sessions check every chunk (AES-GCM tags on the relay, DTLS on direct links) but compute no whole-file checksum; publish a SHA-256 for critical files.
- Speed is limited by the sender's upload bandwidth and, when relayed, by the relay path.
